item.title: Adding Herdr Support to Your Own Agent: Three Kinds of Report, --seq Monotonicity, the Four Hard Constraints on a Resume Command, and How to Test Without Touching Your Normal Session
item.description: If you are building a coding agent, you can make it a first-class citizen in Herdr from your own code — no pull request to Herdr, no waiting for a Herdr release. This article covers the three reports and nothing else: state (pane report-agent --state working/idle/blocked), resume command (pane report-agent with the command after --, or pane report-agent-session), and release on exit (pane release-agent). Plus the four environment variables, why --seq must increase across sessions and restarts or your reports are silently dropped, the four hard constraints on a resume command and the invalid_resume_argv / resume_not_accepted error codes, why the integration must never block your agent, CLI versus raw socket, the Prime Agent reference implementation, and testing restoration in a separate named session.

item.title: All 18 Official Herdr Integrations: Which File Each Installs, Which Config It Touches, Where State Comes From, and the Local Pi and Hermes Situation
item.description: Installing an integration is not how Herdr recognises your agent — detection is automatic. Integrations exist so Herdr can resume the same session after a server restart, and six of them additionally report agent state. This article walks all 18 targets: which file each writes, which config it edits, which environment variable overrides the directory, whether the directory must already exist, and whether state still comes from screen reading. Plus minimum integration versions for native session restore, Claude v10's SessionStart source whitelist, OMP competing with Pi over the extensions directory, OpenCode's three files and V1/V2 differences, why Devin/Droid/Qoder still rely on screen reading, MastraCode having no fallback, Grok's self-contained hooks.json, coexisting with report-metadata, and the measured state of Pi and Hermes on this machine.

item.title: Herdr's Agent State Model: Who Decides the Five States, How the Detection Manifest Works, and Why VMs and Sandboxes Block Detection
item.description: Herdr's agent state has three sources: screen reading (the detection manifest), integration reports, and agent self-reporting. This article clarifies the precedence and each source's failure conditions, using real herdr agent explain output from herdr 0.9.2 on this machine — pi's manifest has exactly two rules (whole_recent matching the literal Working... and bottom_non_empty_lines(12) matching a braille-spinner border regex), plus what fallback_reason: default_known_agent_idle_fallback actually means; why blocked is deliberately strict, why Codex falls back to unknown; the HERDR_AGENT and HERDR_PROCESS_DETECTION=child-groups escape valves for VMs and sandboxes; remote manifest auto-update versus local override precedence; state rollup and custom labels.

item.title: Herdr's Three Remote Work Paths: Run herdr over SSH, the --remote Thin Client, or Mobile SSH — How to Choose
item.description: The official principle is 'run Herdr where the work lives, attach from wherever you are'. This article compares the real differences between the three remote paths: SSH in and run herdr (tmux-style, simplest, but entirely remote and blind to your local clipboard), herdr --remote (the remote server owns the panes and streams, your local Herdr draws the UI with local theme and keybindings, and image clipboard paste can be bridged), and mobile SSH (no app and no web dashboard needed, the TUI adapts to a narrow screen); plus direct terminal attach via herdr agent attach / terminal attach, where the remote binary comes from, whether versions must match, manage_ssh_config and ControlPersist, and why passphrase-protected keys need ssh-add first.

item.title: Connecting Herdr to Machines: Local and Saved SSH Machines in One Window, a Cross-Machine Agent View, Independent Reconnect
item.description: Put local work and remote agents in the same Herdr window: the interactive discovery flow of herdr machine add and its naming rules, one profile mapping to exactly one remote session, client/server compatibility negotiation and approval-based installation, who streams and who only updates state when you switch machines, the dimmed-cache semantics on connection loss, the three connection states Reconnecting / Attention (!auth, !error) / saved-machine file error, SSH authentication recovery (machine status, machine reconnect, ControlPersist 600), and the easiest trap to fall into — ID scoping: w1:p1 can exist on two machines, so remote automation must carry the --machine prefix.

item.title: Herdr's Five Session-State Paths: detach, Snapshot Restore, History Replay, Agent-Native resume, and live handoff
item.description: 'After I close the window / drop SSH / upgrade Herdr / reboot the machine, is my agent still there?' has five different answers. This article takes each Herdr state path apart: live persistence (processes keep running after detach), snapshot restore (layout returns but processes do not, including session-backups recovery copies and the 48 session-snapshots layout copies), pane screen history replay (an experimental feature, off by default), native agent session restore (on by default, with the minimum integration version and resume command for all 18 agents), and live handoff (experimental, opt-in); plus a priority and enablement recommendation for the four paths.

item.title: Herdr Keyboard Control: the Prefix Key, Five Keys to Learn First, copy mode, and a prefix-free Scheme That Does Not Fight Back
item.description: The complete breakdown of Herdr's keyboard layer: why the prefix key exists (the OS, the outer terminal and the program in the pane all claim keystrokes), the five keys worth learning first (prefix+c/v/minus/h-j-k-l/w/q), the full pane/tab/workspace binding table, the editing keys of Herdr's own text fields, copy-mode movement and search rules; the [keys] binding syntax (prefix may be an array, one action may bind several keys, named punctuation, indexed 1..9), the four [[keys.command]] types popup/pane/shell/plugin_action, and the official ctrl+alt prefix-free scheme measured across 10 terminals along with the combinations you must avoid.

item.title: Herdr's Mouse-First Workflow: Create a Workspace and Run Your First Agent Without Touching a Single Binding
item.description: Herdr is mouse-native: click panes/tabs/workspaces to focus, drag split borders to resize, right-click menus to split and create, drag-select to copy, double-click to select a token, Ctrl+click to open links. This article walks the official quick-start order to your first workspace and first agent, marks exactly which actions need the keyboard (only one is genuinely worth learning early: the prefix+g goto picker), and includes real workspace list / agent list output from herdr 0.9.2 on this machine.

item.title: Herdr Core Concepts: session / workspace / tab / pane / agent / mode
item.description: The six-layer Herdr model in one pass: session is the background server's namespace, workspace is the project-level container, tab is a layout, pane is a real terminal, agent is the recognised process (five states and the per-client 'seen' semantics), mode decides where keystrokes go among terminal/prefix/navigate. Includes a real session.json and herdr agent list from this machine, plus a granularity decision table for when to open a new pane / tab / workspace / session.

item.title: Installing and Verifying Herdr: Three Platforms, Five Channels, and How to Prove It Worked
item.description: Install herdr 0.9.2 on macOS / Linux / Windows: the real commands for all five channels (installer script, Homebrew, mise, Nix, manual download) and how each one upgrades; how to switch between the stable and preview channels and why an old Windows preview install cannot switch back; how to read every field of herdr status; and exactly what appears under ~/.local/bin, ~/.config/herdr and ~/.local/state/herdr once it is installed. Includes a failure triage table.

item.title: What Herdr Is: Why tmux Stopped Being Enough
item.description: Herdr is 'the runtime your coding agents live on': a Rust Apache-2.0 project where a background server holds the real terminals and the TUI / CLI / plain SSH session are just clients attached to it. What it adds over tmux is semantics — agent state (blocked / working / done / idle), attaching straight to a single agent, and a read-send-wait API for scripts and agents. This article shows the difference using real output from herdr 0.9.2 on this machine, and is honest about who does not need it.

item.title: Module 3: Agent Integrations (the state model, the 18 official integrations, adding support for your own agent)
item.description: A complete account of Herdr's agent awareness: who decides the five states, how the detection manifest and screen detection work, why VM and sandbox wrappers block detection, the precise semantics of blocked, state rollup and custom labels; installing and debugging the 18 official integrations (Pi, Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Devin, Droid, Kimi, OpenCode, Kilo, Hermes, Qoder, Qwen, Letta, Cursor, MastraCode, Antigravity, Grok, OMP); and how your own agent can report state and a resume command. Baseline herdr 0.9.2 stable.

item.title: Module 2: Remote and Multi-Machine (Local + SSH in one window, the three remote paths)
item.description: Manage Local and saved SSH machines in a single Herdr window: adding, editing and removing machines, the merged agent view, independent reconnect per connection; and how to choose among the three remote paths (SSH in and run herdr, the herdr --remote thin client, mobile SSH) — the differences are bigger than they look, especially clipboard and theme ownership. Baseline herdr 0.9.2 stable.

item.title: Module 1: Daily Workflow (mouse-first, keyboard, session state)
item.description: Everyday Herdr use: the mouse-first workflow (clicking panes, dragging split borders, right-click menus), the ctrl+b prefix and a prefix-free keybinding scheme, and the precise differences between the five state paths: detach / snapshot restore / history replay / agent-native resume / live handoff. Baseline herdr 0.9.2 stable.

item.title: Module 0: Getting to Know Herdr (the Terminal Workspace Manager)
item.description: What Herdr actually is, why tmux stopped being enough, how to install it on macOS / Linux / Windows and prove to yourself it went well, and the six-layer concept model: session / workspace / tab / pane / agent / mode. Baseline herdr 0.9.2 stable.

item.title: The Herdr Practical Guide: A Terminal Workspace for AI Coding Agents
item.description: A hands-on column built on herdr 0.9.2 stable: why tmux stopped being enough, mouse-first multiplexing, agent state awareness (working/blocked/done), Local plus SSH machines in one window, the 18 official agent integrations (including a live check of Pi and Hermes on this machine), CLI and socket API orchestration, plugins and the marketplace. Every command output here comes from a real machine.
